analysis.one_liner: Lets states set up their own universal health care systems using existing federal health money.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in five House committees with no action since its July 2025 introduction, with 35 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state apply to bundle together the federal health money now spent on its residents — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, federal employee and military coverage, and premium tax credits — and use it to run a state-run universal health plan covering everyone. The state plan must cover every resident at costs at least as low as the federal programs it replaces, must cover reproductive health care including abortion, and must aim for 95% coverage within five years or risk losing the waiver. The bill does not itself create any state plan; it only opens a legal door that has not existed, since current law does not let states fold Medicare and employer-based coverage into a state system.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of any state that chooses to apply — including the roughly 26 million uninsured Americans — would gain a path to coverage with no or low out-of-pocket costs, since the state plan must cover all residents and match the affordability of the federal programs it replaces. Lower-income households now paying ACA premiums or Medicaid cost-sharing gain the most. States that want single-payer but have been blocked by federal law (ERISA preemption, rules against buying coverage for Medicare and federal employees) gain the legal authority they have lacked, as Vermont's 2014 effort showed. The bill is optional, so no state or resident is forced to change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: Any state could apply to set up a publicly administered health plan covering all its residents, with federal money that would have been spent on Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE in that state funneled to the state instead — including amounts for caseload growth, adjusted for medical inflation.

The state plan must be at least as comprehensive and at least as affordable as the federal programs it replaces, must cover reproductive health care including abortion and gender-affirming care, and must guarantee appeal and complaint rights.
States must plan to cover at least 95% of residents within five years, and an independent panel and five-year public reviews with hearings check whether the state is actually delivering.

States can band together in regional applications, American Indians and Alaska Natives keep their federal protections without being forced to enroll, and any savings a state achieves can be reinvested in health care services.

analysis.who_pays: No one directly, since the bill only authorizes waivers and makes no spending mandatory by itself. In a participating state, the cost would fall on state taxpayers and on anyone whose employer- or private coverage is folded into the state plan, and the private health insurance industry would lose the individual-market business in that state.

drawbacks.text: The federal passthrough covers only the federal programs the state assumes (Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, FEHB, TRICARE); most working-age people get insurance through employers, and federal funding for employer-based coverage (like the tax exclusion) is not part of the deal, so a state would likely have to raise substantial new state taxes to fund universal coverage.

A participating state must cover reproductive health care including abortion and gender-affirming care [S2], a provision that would draw fierce opposition in many states and could complicate federal approval; the ban on selling duplicative coverage also means most private insurance would effectively disappear inside a participating state.

Waivers can be terminated if a state fails to reach 95% coverage after review and a 12-month grace period [S2], so a state that misjudges the financing or enrollment could lose the federal passthrough and face a disruptive transition back.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for states that want universal coverage is real: this clears the main federal legal barriers that have stopped them before, and its funding, benefit, and affordability floors would protect residents during the transition. The costs and risks are also real: federal funding does not automatically include employer-based plan spending, so states could face shortfalls unless they raise taxes; private insurers would lose the individual-market role in adopting states; and Medicare/TRICARE coordination is untested. Honest supporters would acknowledge that success depends entirely on each state's politics and fiscal capacity, and that no state is certain to apply. But as written, it adds a state option without taking anything away from states that stay with the current system.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House on July 15, 2025 and sent to five committees, none of which has acted on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 15, 2025 and referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Education and Workforce committees.
No committee has taken it up, and no vote has occurred; the record after the referral is empty.
It has 35 cosponsors, all House Democrats, in a chamber where Republicans hold 223 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, the party that benefits from the current system — health insurers and other stakeholders who prefer that states lack a route to single-payer — is better off that the bill sits idle; no state has gained a path to universal coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and opponents of single-payer

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; with Republicans holding 223 of 436 House seats, the bill cannot advance without their scheduling it.

against.name: Chairs of the five committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Have taken no action on the bill since it was referred to their committees on July 15, 2025 — no hearings or markup are in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; Republicans hold 223 House seats, so a bill this partisan cannot reach the floor in this Congress.

industries.note: In a participating state, the state plan replaces ACA exchange plans, Medicaid managed care, and much employer-style coverage, and the state must restrict duplicative private insurance; insurers could still administer the plan as contractors, but their role as sellers of coverage largely disappears. This loss is conditional — only in states that apply and are approved.

A state universal plan would make nearly all residents paying patients, cutting uncompensated care, but provider payment rates and bargaining power would be set by the state plan rather than by negotiations with insurers.
The bill does not use federal authority to negotiate or cap drug prices in participating states, so drug pricing is largely untouched even as coverage becomes universal.

The waiver frees states from ERISA preemption and employer-mandate penalties within the state, letting employers shift coverage costs to the state plan; workers gain portability but the financing burden moves to state taxes.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic support, no committee action months after referral, and Republican control of the House, the bill is very likely to die without a vote, as previous versions of this proposal have. Its realistic function is to keep the idea on the record for future Congresses.
